subject: English Language
source: CISCE ICSE English Language (Paper 1) 2023 - Analysis of Pupil Performance (raw/LangPPA-23.pdf)

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
Write an original short story in which two children and their school teacher are the main characters.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: The story must be original. All three characters should have a definite role.
key_points: Two children and their school teacher are the main characters
All three characters have a definite role
common_errors: First-person narrative instead of a story
Plot lifted from known authors or the comprehension
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Stories lacked creativity; many wrote a first-person narrative instead of a short story. Some lifted language and plots from popular children's authors or from the comprehension passage, changing only names. 'Original' was misunderstood by a few. Characters were underdeveloped; dialogue did not advance the story; endings rambled or were missing. Short scripts and overlong essays were common; no paragraphs.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
Imagine a situation where you get an opportunity to change one thing in your school. What would it be? Why do you want to change it? How would you bring about the change?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Only one change required - what change. Why necessary, benefits. How - A plan on how to bring about the change is to be included. E.g., Change in timing or Write a letter, take an opinion poll.
key_points: Why it is necessary / its benefits
A plan for how to bring about the change (e.g. write a letter, take an opinion poll)
common_errors: Wrote about changing schools or own behaviour
No plan for implementing the change
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many misread the topic and wrote about changing the school itself, their own behaviour, or listed several changes and ignored the rest of the question. The plan for bringing about the change was largely missing. Elaborate introductions wasted time; some posed as the Principal; impractical changes were proposed.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
'School examinations do not test intelligence.' Express your views either for or against this statement.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Views either for or against are to be accepted. The candidate should take a clear stand and give valid reasons for whatever stand he / she takes. Credit to be given for a cohesive well-constructed logical argument and ideas based on logical reasoning and personal experience.
key_points: Takes one clear stand, either for or against
Cohesive, logical argument drawing on reasoning and personal experience
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Some argued both sides without a definitive stance. Logical reasoning was often missing; arguments were repetitive, too few and not backed by illustration or example. The tone was at times aggrieved rather than objective and persuasive.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
You are a regular visitor to your school library. Describe your library. Give details of the familiar sights. What do you see and feel as different students come in and check out the books? Why is this place so important?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Brief description of library, shelves, books, magazines, quiet, hush, librarian, students entering browsing, reading. Importance of reading in a student's life.
key_points: Brief description of the library: shelves, books, magazines, quiet, hush, librarian
Students entering, browsing, reading; what the narrator sees and feels
Importance of the library / reading in a student's life
common_errors: Benefits of reading without describing the library
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: The most popular choice. Even able writers merely listed familiar sights (yellow walls, brown shelves). The library as one quiet room in a busy building was not evoked; feelings and students' reactions were not brought out; why the library matters was not in focus. Some wrote on the benefits of reading without describing the library.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
Study the picture given below. Write a story or a description or an account of what it suggests to you. Your composition may be about the subject of the picture, or you may take suggestions from it; however, there must be a clear connection between the picture and your composition.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Accept a wide interpretation. Any relevant ideas taken from the picture should be accepted. However, a mere itemization / listing / description of the picture is to be penalized.
key_points: Clear connection between the picture and the composition
Wide interpretation accepted: story, description or account
Not a mere itemisation/listing/description of the picture
common_errors: Began 'This picture shows...' and listed elements
Picture not used as the central idea
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Most began 'This picture shows us that...' and listed its elements. A connection between the picture and the composition was lacking in most cases; the picture was not used as the central theme. Some copied the question or passage; colloquialisms and contractions were used.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation
penalised: Mere itemisation / listing / description of the picture

marking_schemes.question_text: You have had to shift to a new house recently. Write a letter to your grandmother telling her what you miss about your old house. Tell her also what you like about your new house and what you plan to do to make it comfortable for yourself.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
Format (Friendly/Informal letter)
Content
What you miss: e.g. friends / locality / gardens / space / quiet (Any two)
What you like: e.g. new / fresh / gardens / locality / space / own room (Any two)
What you plan to do: e.g. decorate / plant / paint (Any one)
Expression: Language, syntax, vocabulary
Format (as printed in the 2023 scheme) - Friendly letter: Address, Date, Salutation, Subscription, First name. Formal letter: From address, Date, To address, Salutation, Subscription, Name + surname / one initial + surname.
key_points: What you miss (any two): e.g. friends / locality / gardens / space / quiet
What you like (any two): e.g. new / fresh / gardens / locality / space / own room
What you plan to do (any one): e.g. decorate / plant / paint
common_errors: Wrote about school instead of home
Plan for making the home comfortable missing
Formal subscription ('Yours faithfully') in an informal letter
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Format: incomplete address, wrong date or missing year; odd salutations (dear grandfather/friend/parent); missing commas; subscriptions such as 'Yours faithfully', 'Yours truly', 'Your's lovingly', 'ABC'; surname added to the first name; mixed formats. Content: some wrote about the old school instead of the old home, or about themselves, friends and the new school; many omitted what they missed or how they would make the new home comfortable; points were jumbled or one point over-developed. Some copied the points from the topic.

format_elements: Date (day, month written in full, year)
Salutation addressing the recipient by name or relation (e.g. Dear Riya / Dear Grandma)
Body: opening sentence, content paragraphs, closing sentence
Subscription (e.g. Yours lovingly / Yours affectionately), no apostrophe in 'Yours'

marking_schemes.question_text: A certain book / chapter has been included in your syllabus. You have heard that a film version is now available. Write a letter to the Manager of a film theatre near your school, requesting that the film be shown. Tell him / her why it will be beneficial to the students.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
Format (Formal letter)
Content
Name of book / chapter: e.g. Boy with Striped Pyjamas
Request to show: e.g. Please arrange / show / have morning matinee / holiday
Why beneficial to students: e.g. clearer understanding / come alive / depth
Expression: Language, syntax, vocabulary
Format (as printed in the 2023 scheme) - Friendly letter: Address, Date, Salutation, Subscription, First name. Formal letter: From address, Date, To address, Salutation, Subscription, Name + surname / one initial + surname.
key_points: Name of book / chapter: e.g. Boy with Striped Pyjamas
Request to show: e.g. Please arrange / show / have morning matinee / holiday
Why beneficial to students: e.g. clearer understanding / come alive / depth
common_errors: Benefits framed as fun, not learning
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Format: no 'To' address, or designation/organisation missing; school name or XYZ; incomplete or numeric dates; wrong months; 'Respected Sir/Madam/Ma'am'; 'Yours sincerely' or 'Yours affectionately' instead of 'Yours faithfully'; 'Your's'. Content: many did not name the book or chapter or a specific show; benefits were not explained or focused on the 'fun' of an outing. Expression: informal language and faulty construction.

writing_task.recipient: The Manager of a film theatre
format_elements: Date (day, month written in full, year)
Receiver's address beginning with the designation, then organisation and city
Salutation (Sir / Madam / Dear Sir / Dear Madam), not 'Respected Sir'
Body: opening sentence, content paragraphs, closing sentence

examples: Please arrange / show / have morning matinee / holiday

marking_schemes.question_text: Write a notice to be put up in your school informing the pupils of Classes IX and X about the Remedial Classes to be held after the school hours and asking them to register their names for it.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
Creative Title: Ready to Learn / Refresh Revise, Relearn
Event: Remedial Classes / Registration for Remedial Classes
Date: 10 - 15 March 2023 (Accept single date or several dates)
Time: 2.00 p.m. - 5.00 p.m. (after school hours)
Venue: smaller place to larger
Participate: All pupils who wish to avail of / have been nominated for / etc. the remedial class/es should give their names to the Vice Principal/etc. on or before ...
key_points: Creative Title: Ready to Learn / Refresh Revise, Relearn
Event: Remedial Classes / Registration for Remedial Classes
Date: 10 - 15 March 2023 (Accept single date or several dates)
Participate: All pupils who wish to avail of / have been nominated for / etc. the remedial class/es should give their names to the Vice Principal/etc. on or before ...
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Creative titles were missing, inappropriate or long. Many misread 'Remedial' as 'Remedy' (titles like 'First Aid') or as a competition, jubilee event or sports. Notices were written as paragraphs. Event dates were too far ahead or on the exam date (should be 10-14 days after the notice); registration dates too close to or after the event. Details were interchanged or incomplete (no year, vague venue).

examples: Remedial Classes / Registration for Remedial Classes
10 - 15 March 2023 (Accept single date or several dates)
All pupils who wish to avail of / have been nominated for / etc. the remedial class/es should give their names to the Vice Principal/etc. on or before ...

penalised: Words from the question used in the creative title (recommended against)

marking_schemes.question_text:
Your school is holding Remedial Classes for the pupils of Classes IX and X after school hours.
Write an email to the Principal of a neighbouring school inviting their pupils to attend the classes if they so wish. Give all details of the classes to be held.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
E-mail id (recipient; official, with @ and provider)
Subject
Salutation
Opening sentence
Closing sentence
Subscription
Expression - All details of the notice are to be included in the e-mail.
key_points: E-mail id (recipient; official, with @ and provider)
Expression - All details of the notice are to be included in the e-mail.
common_errors: Invited the Principal instead of the pupils
Details do not match the notice
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Incorrect email ids ('principle'); personal ids; subject missing; unclear opening sentence; missing closing sentence; opening/closing overlapping the content. 'Respected sir/Ma'am' or 'thank you' and a name. Date, venue, time missing or the exam date given; notice and email dates not matching. Some invited the Principal instead of the pupils.

writing_task.recipient: The Principal of a neighbouring school
format_elements: E-mail id (recipient; official, with @ and provider)
writing_task.expression_criteria: Expression - All details of the notice are to be included in the e-mail.
writing_task.question_text_note: Event context from 3(i) prefixed so this question stands alone.

marking_schemes.question_text:
For each word given below choose the correct meaning (as used in the passage) from the options provided:
1. summoned (line 1)
options: (a) totalled
(b) ordered
(c) requested
(d) shout
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (b) ordered
marking_schemes.model_answer: (b) ordered
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Several ignored context: 'summoned' was taken as 'requested', or as a sum total; some wrote words outside the options or mismatched letters.

stimulus.text:
That huge bell never stopped ringing. It got us out of bed, it summoned us for meals, it rang between class periods, it sent us unwillingly to bed.

One morning it failed to ring, or rather, there was no bell to ring. Someone had removed it, and it wasn't found till late in the afternoon.

What a glorious day! As there was no bell to rouse us, everyone got up late, and there was no morning PT. Some of us missed breakfast too. The teachers got confused and mixed up their classes. How could the school manage without it? Confusion reigned.

Of course, no one owned up. It could have meant expulsion. Some suspicion fell on the Sports Captain because of our aversion to morning PT, but nothing could be proved.

No one was very anxious to find the bell - we were quite happy without it - but it was finally discovered hanging from a branch of one of the trees.

'It may have been Mr. Sharma,' surmised Brian. Mr. Sharma, our Maths teacher, was known to walk in his sleep. And sleepwalkers did funny things sometimes.

'It could be Mool Chand himself,' suggested Cyrus Satralkar.

Mool Chand was the school chowkidar, who also had the job of banging the brass bell at appointed times.

'Why would he throw it away?'

'He must be as fed up with ringing it as we are of hearing it.' This was my theory. 'Perhaps he wants a rise in salary.'

The identity of the culprit remained a mystery. Happily, the senior Hockey team went on a winning spree against all corners, and our month-end exits were restored.

But soon there was another sensation.

A girl was admitted to our class!

The boys were scandalized. No girl had ever studied in our school before. We protested.

'What's the problem?' asked Mr. Knight, our class master. 'Haven't you seen a girl before?'

'But - but. Sir...' Tata was our spokesman. 'How will we concentrate on our studies?'

'When did you ever concentrate on your studies, Tata?'

'Are we going co-ed, sir?' Adams wanted to know.

'Not at all,' said Mr. Knight. 'This is a special case. She is the school accounts manager's daughter, and he can't afford the Girls school fees. So, I'm sure you'll make her feel very welcome.'

The accountant was a popular man who also ran the school's tuck shop and allowed most of us a certain amount of credit. All our objections faded away.

At first, Sunita, our new entrant, was a bit of a distraction because, although she was very shy and demure, she had lovely curly hair, bright eyes, pink cheeks and a smile for everyone. All the boys were very polite and attentive to her and Brian in particular was always ready to help her.
stimulus.line_references: Line numbers in questions refer to the printed paper's margin numbering.

marking_schemes.question_text:
For each word given below choose the correct meaning (as used in the passage) from the options provided:
2. aversion (line 10)
options: (a) hatred
(b) fear
(c) politeness
(d) creation
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (a) hatred
marking_schemes.model_answer: (a) hatred
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: 'Aversion' was taken as 'politeness' by some and 'fear' by many.

marking_schemes.question_text:
Answer the following questions briefly in your own words:
(a) Why did no one confess to having removed the missing bell?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Feared expulsion
marking_schemes.model_answer: Feared expulsion
common_errors: Wrote about the advantages of no bell
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many gave a general answer (they were happy the bell was gone) or missed 'fear of expulsion'; 'punishment' is not an adequate substitute for 'expulsion'.

'Not at all,' said Mr. Knight. 'This is a special case. She is the school accounts manager's daughter, and he can't afford the Girls school fees. So, I'm sure you'll make her feel very welcome.'

stimulus.text:
That huge bell never stopped ringing. It got us out of bed, it summoned us for meals, it rang between class periods, it sent us unwillingly to bed.

One morning it failed to ring, or rather, there was no bell to ring. Someone had removed it, and it wasn't found till late in the afternoon.

What a glorious day! As there was no bell to rouse us, everyone got up late, and there was no morning PT. Some of us missed breakfast too. The teachers got confused and mixed up their classes. How could the school manage without it? Confusion reigned.

Of course, no one owned up. It could have meant expulsion. Some suspicion fell on the Sports Captain because of our aversion to morning PT, but nothing could be proved.

No one was very anxious to find the bell - we were quite happy without it - but it was finally discovered hanging from a branch of one of the trees.

'It may have been Mr. Sharma,' surmised Brian. Mr. Sharma, our Maths teacher, was known to walk in his sleep. And sleepwalkers did funny things sometimes.

'It could be Mool Chand himself,' suggested Cyrus Satralkar.

Mool Chand was the school chowkidar, who also had the job of banging the brass bell at appointed times.

'Why would he throw it away?'

'He must be as fed up with ringing it as we are of hearing it.' This was my theory. 'Perhaps he wants a rise in salary.'

The identity of the culprit remained a mystery. Happily, the senior Hockey team went on a winning spree against all corners, and our month-end exits were restored.

But soon there was another sensation.

A girl was admitted to our class!

The boys were scandalized. No girl had ever studied in our school before. We protested.

'What's the problem?' asked Mr. Knight, our class master. 'Haven't you seen a girl before?'

'But - but. Sir...' Tata was our spokesman. 'How will we concentrate on our studies?'

'When did you ever concentrate on your studies, Tata?'

'Are we going co-ed, sir?' Adams wanted to know.

'Not at all,' said Mr. Knight. 'This is a special case. She is the school accounts manager's daughter, and he can't afford the Girls school fees. So, I'm sure you'll make her feel very welcome.'

The accountant was a popular man who also ran the school's tuck shop and allowed most of us a certain amount of credit. All our objections faded away.

At first, Sunita, our new entrant, was a bit of a distraction because, although she was very shy and demure, she had lovely curly hair, bright eyes, pink cheeks and a smile for everyone. All the boys were very polite and attentive to her and Brian in particular was always ready to help her.

Points:

marking_schemes.question_text:
Fill in each of the numbered blanks with the correct form of the word given in brackets. Do not copy the passage but write in correct serial order the word or phrase appropriate to the blank space.
Example: (0) One night four college students ______ (be) out partying late and did not study for the test scheduled for the next day. Answer: were
In the morning, they (1) ______ (think) of a plan. They (2) ______ (make) themselves look dirty with grease and dirt. Then they (3) ______ (go) to the Dean and (4) ______ (say) they (5) ______ (go) out to a wedding last night and on their way back the tyre of their car burst and they had to push the car all the way back. The Dean thought for a minute and said that they could have the re-test after three days. They (6) ______ (thank) him and said they would be ready. On the day of the test, they were made to sit in separate rooms. They agreed as they (7) ______ (prepare) well. But they (8) ______ (get) a rude shock!
marking_schemes.scheme_text: [0. were] (1) thought  (2) made  (3) went  (4) said  (5) had gone  (6) thanked  (7) had prepared  (8) got
marking_schemes.model_answer:
(1) thought
(2) made
(3) went
(4) said
(5) had gone
(6) thanked
(7) had prepared
(8) got
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Common errors: (1) 'thinked', (5) 'went' and (7) 'prepared' - simple past confused with past perfect.

(c) of

1: Discuss short-story format; stress originality; hint at theme, characters and setting in the introduction
Practise plot development, dialogue and logical, open-ended or cliffhanger endings
Explain the difference between short story and narrative writing
Teach students to identify and address every part of the question; use rough drafts; respect word limits
Argumentative essays: a hook, 3-4 planned points with examples, a strong stance, a strong conclusion
Descriptive essays: rich description rather than listing
Picture composition: find the central idea; avoid itemising
2: Teach correct format (address, date, salutation, subscription) and the formal/informal difference
Read the question carefully and develop every point; identify premise, problems and solutions
Avoid contractions, short forms and colloquial language
3: Explain why a creative (phrasal) title is needed
Give date, venue (smaller and larger) and time correctly
Explain registration details and the gap before the event
Teach official email-id components; copy the event into the subject
Notice and email details must match; clarify host vs invitee roles
4: Read words in context; regular vocabulary and MCQ practice
Quote exactly one appropriate sentence when asked
Use a grid for summaries; keep sequence; leave out irrelevant detail
5: Teach verb forms and tenses logically
Demonstrate prepositions with everyday examples; adverbs and phrasal verbs
Teach rules of synthesis; neither-nor vs either-or
Practise voice, comparison, reported speech, 'too', 'Hardly...when', tense change

difficult_topics: Essay word limit (300-350): short scripts or overlong essays; copying the question or passage
Informal letter: making oneself comfortable in a new home; uneven coverage of parts
Formal letter: making specific requests in formal language
Notice: topic not understood, written as a paragraph; notice-email connection missed
Comprehension vocabulary and analytical questions; quoting a sentence
confusions: Letters: likes/dislikes between the two homes; naming a specific chapter
Notice-email: what remedial classes are and who the host is
